title: Timing of Delayed Retinal Pathology in Patients Presenting with Acute Posterior Vitreous Detachment in the IRIS Registry (Intelligent Research in Sight)
condition_or_topic: Delayed retinal breaks and detachments after acute posterior vitreous detachment (PVD)
clinical_background: Symptomatic PVD can be accompanied by a retinal tear at presentation; published estimates range from 8% to 22%. Retinal pathology may also be overlooked during the initial examination or develop later as PVD progresses. The optimal timing of reassessment remains uncertain, and follow-up practices vary according to examination findings, clinician preference, and ocular risk factors.
objectives: Determine how often delayed or initially missed retinal breaks or detachments occur after acute PVD and measure the time from the initial diagnosis to their detection.
Assess whether ocular risk factors are associated with earlier or more frequent delayed retinal pathology.
Examine the timing of delayed pathology according to whether the treating physician is a retinal specialist or a nonretinal specialist.

Evaluate the incidence of delayed or initially missed retinal breaks or detachments within 1 year after the initial PVD diagnosis and the final visual acuity closest to 1 year after that diagnosis ( 3 months).
study_design: Nonrandomized retrospective cohort study using de-identified data from the IRIS Registry. The analysis used the database version dated December 18, 2020.

population.description: The cohort comprised 434 046 eyes from 367 645 patients with a documented initial PVD and no retinal break or detachment recorded on the index date. Baseline variables included VA, lens status, laterality, vitreous hemorrhage, myopia, prior retinal break or detachment in the fellow eye, lattice degeneration, demographic characteristics, smoking status, geographic region, insurance, and treating physician subspecialty.
inclusion_criteria: An eye had a PVD diagnosis recorded between July 1, 2013, and December 31, 2018, using ICD-9 code 379.21 or ICD-10 code H43.81.
Extended ophthalmoscopy was recorded under codes 92225/92226; the study specifies a 2-week interval relative to the initial PVD diagnosis.
exclusion_criteria: <6 months of preceding IRIS Registry data.
<1 year of follow-up after the index event.
No recorded National Provider Identifier linked to the extended ophthalmoscopy.
A retinal break or detachment recorded on the index date.
Previous vitrectomy or a previously treated retinal break in the eye.
population.care_setting: Practices contributing records to the IRIS Registry, including retinal specialists, comprehensive ophthalmologists, and optometrists.

comparators: Eyes examined by retinal specialists versus eyes examined by nonretinal specialists; retinal-specialist status was based on the ophthalmologist’s self-designation in the American Academy of Ophthalmology membership database.
Eyes with at least 1 specified high-risk ocular characteristic versus eyes without those characteristics.

primary: Time in days from the initial PVD diagnosis to a delayed or missed retinal break or detachment, also assessed according to whether the treating physician was a retinal specialist.
secondary: Incidence of delayed or missed retinal breaks or detachments within 1 year after the index event.
Final VA measured closest to 1 year after the index event; the document also specifies a 3-month interval without a discernible direction.

statistical_methods: A multivariable shared frailty survival model clustered by patient assessed baseline predictors of delayed retinal break or detachment within 1 year; the reported analysis adjusted for age, gender, and race/ethnicity. An exploratory analysis examined the timing of delayed pathology in eyes with high-risk ocular characteristics. Differences in means were tested with an independent, 2-tailed t test. The stated significance threshold is P 0.05; no comparison operator is specified in the document.
follow_up: At least 1 year after the index event was required for inclusion; delayed retinal pathology was assessed within 1 year. At least 6 months of preceding registry data was also required.
interpretation: After an initial PVD diagnosis, delayed or initially undetected retinal pathology was identified in 2.42% of included eyes. The median intervals to retinal break and detachment were 42 and 51 days, respectively. Eyes with at least 1 of the specified ocular risk factors had shorter median intervals of 34 and 39 days; for eyes documented with vitreous hemorrhage alone, the median interval to retinal break was 14 days. In the adjusted analysis, vitreous hemorrhage (HR, 9.30; 95% CI, 8.50e10.2), a history of retinal break or detachment in the fellow eye (HR, 3.91; 95% CI, 3.64e4.20), lattice degeneration (HR, 2.61; 95% CI, 2.35e2.90), and myopia (HR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.33e1.53) were associated with greater risk. Retinal breaks were identified sooner among eyes examined by nonretinal specialists than among those examined by retinal specialists (median = 37 days versus median = 42 days; P < 0.001). The corresponding difference for retinal detachment was not significant (median = 56 days versus median = 49 days; P = 0.39). The authors suggest that differences in symptom counseling, return precautions, or established follow-up patterns may contribute to the timing difference for breaks.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier studies reported delayed retinal pathology in 1% to 3% of eyes after initial PVD, consistent with this study's 2.42%. The 2019 American Academy of Ophthalmology Preferred Practice Pattern Guidelines advocated reassessment within 2 months, or within 1 to 2 weeks for eyes with vitreous hemorrhage or after treatment of an acute retinal tear; the authors consider their findings generally consistent with those guidelines. In a study by Seider et al involving 7522 patients, the median interval to delayed break or detachment was 22 days, suggesting that reassessment might be needed earlier than the general 2-month interval. That study identified male sex, age < 60 years, vitreous hemorrhage, lattice degeneration, a fellow-eye history of retinal tear or detachment, and previous cataract surgery as risk factors. In a study by Uhr et al involving 7999 eyes, 2.6% developed a delayed break at a median of 35 days, and vitreous hemorrhage and male sex were significant risk factors.
clinical_implications: A retinal break or detachment can emerge or be recognized after an initial PVD examination, with potentially permanent consequences for vision; its absence at presentation does not remove the need to consider later pathology.
Vitreous hemorrhage, lattice degeneration, fellow-eye retinal break or detachment, and myopia identify eyes in which delayed pathology may occur more frequently and sooner.

In eyes with vitreous hemorrhage, later recognition of a break or detachment may reflect progression of PVD or inadequate visualization of the vitreous base. B-scan ultrasonography may help when added to a detailed examination, but its reported sensitivity and positive predictive value vary widely (24%e 100%) with the technology and examiner.
Because myopia is associated with retinal pathology and its prevalence has increased, knowledge of precorrection refractive error can inform risk stratification in acute PVD.
practice_implications: The authors recommend at least one repeat examination within the first 6 weeks for all patients after an initial PVD examination, with earlier and more frequent examinations for eyes with higher-risk features.
For patients with vitreous hemorrhage, the authors advise frequent reassessment and consideration of early vitrectomy to prevent worsening pathology.
The examination described as standard care includes slit lamp biomicroscopy and indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression, with B-scan ultrasonography when visualization is inadequate.
limitations: ICD or common procedural technology coding errors in the IRIS Registry could have led to incorrect inclusion or exclusion of eyes.

The acute PVD diagnosis relied on ICD codes and could not be checked individually against records, OCT, or ultrasonographic imaging. Coding extended ophthalmoscopy preferentially for eyes considered more suspicious could have introduced selection bias and resulted in incorrect exclusions.

The available data did not permit quantification of the number of retinal tears, the severity of vitreous hemorrhage, or the degree of lattice degeneration or myopia. Severity-based analyses might have clarified differences in incidence and timing.
Retinal pathology recorded after the initial examination might already have been present but overlooked.
The methodology could not assess photopsias, myodesopsias, or examination findings that were not captured by codes, such as vitreous pigment.
strengths: The authors describe this as the largest-known cohort used to examine the incidence and timing of delayed retinal pathology associated with PVD.
The broad, heterogeneous data set included electronic health records from retinal specialists, comprehensive ophthalmologists, and optometrists.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that repeat assessment after an initial PVD is necessary to identify retinal pathology detected later or missed initially. They recommend at least one further examination within the first 6 weeks for all patients, with earlier and more frequent examinations when higher-risk ocular features are present.
narrative_summary: This nonrandomized retrospective cohort study used the IRIS Registry to examine when retinal breaks or detachments were diagnosed after an initial PVD without same-day retinal pathology. The analysis included 434 046 eyes meeting the study criteria; 10 518 (2.42%) received a diagnosis of delayed or missed retinal break or detachment within 1 year. Median time from the initial PVD to a break was 42 days, and median time to detachment was 51 days. In the adjusted survival analysis, vitreous hemorrhage showed the strongest association with subsequent pathology (HR, 9.30; 95% CI, 8.50e10.2), followed by a history of break or detachment in the fellow eye (HR, 3.91; 95% CI, 3.64e4.20), lattice degeneration (HR, 2.61; 95% CI, 2.35e2.90), and myopia (HR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.33e1.53). Among eyes with at least 1 of these features, median times to break and detachment were 34 and 39 days, respectively; among other eyes, they were 51 and 62 days. The authors advise at least one repeat examination within the first 6 weeks, sooner and more often for higher-risk eyes. They caution that diagnostic coding could be inaccurate and that pathology recorded later may have been missed at the first examination rather than newly developed.

document_sections.heading: Objective:
document_sections.content: The study aimed to establish when retinal pathology is detected after an eye presents with acute posterior vitreous detachment (PVD).

document_sections.heading: Design:
document_sections.content: The authors conducted a retrospective database study.

document_sections.heading: Subjects:
document_sections.content: The study followed patients in the Intelligent Research in Sight (IRIS) registry whose acute PVD was identified through International Classification of Diseases, Ninth and Tenth Revision, codes.

document_sections.heading: Methods:
document_sections.content: The investigators included PVD-coded patients from 2013 to 2018 who also had an extended ophthalmoscopy procedure code. Baseline ocular characteristics comprised visual acuity, lens status, vitreous hemorrhage, myopia, lattice degeneration, and the treating physician’s subspecialty training.

document_sections.heading: Main Outcome Measures:
document_sections.content: The principal measure was the number of days from the initial PVD to a delayed retinal break or detachment.

document_sections.heading: Results:
document_sections.content: Among 434 046 eligible eyes, 10 518 eyes (2.42%) were diagnosed with a delayed retinal break or detachment after initial PVD. Median time after the initial PVD was 42 (range, 1e365) days for a retinal break and 51 (range, 1e365) days for a detachment. Higher risk of delayed break or detachment was associated with vitreous hemorrhage (hazard ratio [HR], 9.30; 95% confidence interval [CI], 8.50e10.2), a history of retinal break/retinal detachment in the fellow eye (HR, 3.91; 95% CI, 3.64e4.20), lattice degeneration (HR, 2.61; 95% CI, 2.35e2.90), and myopia (HR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.33e1.53).

document_sections.heading: Conclusions:
document_sections.content: A follow-up examination after an initial PVD is needed to identify retinal disease that develops later or was missed initially. For eyes without pathology at presentation, clinicians should consider at least one further examination within 6 weeks, with earlier reassessment when higher-risk features are present.

PVD commonly brings patients to general ophthalmology and retinal clinics and can lead to serious ocular disease. Across cited studies, retinal tears at presentation with symptomatic PVD have been reported in 8% to 22%. Because PVD evolves, retinal pathology can arise after the first examination or escape detection at that visit. The best interval before reassessment remains uncertain and variable, while missing disease can have serious visual consequences. Follow-up timing differs according to examination findings, clinician preference, and ocular risk factors. Using the American Academy of Ophthalmology IRIS Registry (Intelligent Research in Sight), the authors sought to measure the incidence and timing of delayed retinal breaks and detachments in a large, broadly representative population. They also sought to identify ocular factors associated with earlier or more frequent retinal pathology and intended the findings to inform clinical decisions.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: This was a nonrandomized retrospective cohort study conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Because the IRIS Registry held de-identified data, the study was exempt from Institutional Review Board approval. The analysis used the database version dated December 18, 2020. Eligible eyes had a documented PVD (International Classification of Disease, Ninth Revision [ICD-9], 379.21; ICD, Tenth Revision [ICD-10], H43.81) between July 1, 2013, and December 31, 2018, together with extended ophthalmoscopy codes 92225/92226 2 weeks from the index event, which was the first documented PVD diagnosis. Exclusions were age <18 years, <6 months of earlier IRIS Registry data, <1 year of follow-up, or absence of a recorded National Provider Identifier for the extended ophthalmoscopy. Eyes were also excluded if a retinal break (ICD, Ninth Revision, 361.3; ICD, Tenth Revision, H33.30, H33.31, and H33.32) or detachment (ICD, Ninth Revision, 361.0, 361.81, and 361.89; ICD, Tenth Revision, H33.01, H33.02, H33.03, H33.04, H33.05, and H33.4) was coded on the index date, or if they had undergone vitrectomy or treatment for a prior retinal break. Recorded ocular characteristics were presenting visual acuity (VA), lens status, laterality, vitreous hemorrhage, myopia, fellow-eye history of retinal break or detachment, and lattice degeneration. Other characteristics were age, sex, race/ethnicity, smoking status, practice region, insurance, and whether the treating physician was a retinal specialist. Specialist status came from ophthalmologists’ self-designation in the American Academy of Ophthalmology membership database. The primary outcome was days from initial PVD to a break or detachment detected later or missed initially; it was also assessed by retinal versus nonretinal specialist care. Secondary outcomes were the incidence of such pathology within 1 year and the final VA recorded closest to 1 year after the index event ( 3 months).

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: A multivariable shared frailty survival model, clustered by patient and incorporating baseline covariates, assessed evidence of risk factors for retinal break or detachment within 1 year of the initial PVD diagnosis. The stated significance level was P 0.05. Differences between means were tested with an independent, 2-tailed t test.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: Between July 1, 2013, and December 31, 2018, PVD was documented in 12 803 515 distinct eyes; 434 046 eyes remained after the additional eligibility criteria. Table 1 describes cohort size and baseline age and VA for the overall, high-risk, and low-risk groups. Across all included eyes, mean age was 70.6 years (range, 18e106), and mean presenting VA was 0.23 (0.32) logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution. Most patients were White (75.6%) and women (61.6%). Within 1 year, 10 518 eyes (2.42%) received a diagnosis of retinal break or detachment that was delayed or missed at presentation; the reported counts were n = 7241 for breaks and n = 4173 for detachments. The respective median times were 42 and 51 days. For retinal-specialist-examined eyes, median time to a delayed retinal break was 42 days and to detachment was 49 days; for nonretinal-specialist-examined eyes, the corresponding times were 37 and 56 days (P < 0.001 and P = 0.39, respectively). Final mean VA was 0.24 (0.35) logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution overall, 0.25 (0.36) in retinal-specialist-examined eyes, and 0.22 (0.33) in nonretinal-specialist-examined eyes. The text reports that 7474 (77.8%) eyes with a delayed or missed break were examined twice by the same provider; within that subgroup, 5872 (78.5%) were seen by a retinal specialist. Table 2 presents the number of eyes, time to retinal break or detachment, and final VA by examiner specialty and risk group. In a multivariable shared frailty analysis adjusted for age, gender, and race/ethnicity, the ocular covariates with HR > 1 for delayed or missed break or detachment were vitreous hemorrhage (HR, 9.30; 95% CI, 8.50e10.2), fellow-eye history of retinal break/retinal detachment (HR, 3.91; 95% CI, 3.64e4.20), lattice degeneration (HR, 2.61; 95% CI, 2.35e2.90), and myopia (HR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.33e1.53). The authors then explored the timing of pathology in eyes with those features. Of all included eyes, 61 700 (14.2%) had at least 1 of the specified high-risk ocular characteristics; 4177 (6.77%) of those eyes subsequently had a retinal break or detachment. In the high-risk group, median time was 34 days for a break (n = 2954) and 39 days for a detachment (n = 1644). In eyes without those high-risk features, the respective medians were 51 and 62 days. Table 4 details outcomes for individual high-risk features and their combinations, including time to break, time to detachment, and final VA.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: Acute symptomatic PVD can have serious visual consequences without appropriate management. In addition to flashes (photopsias) and floaters (myodesopsias), retinal tears and detachments may cause permanent visual impairment. Retinal tears usually arise at the vitreous base, which extends 2 mm anterior and 4 mm posterior to the ora serrata. Because this region can be hard to visualize, the described standard examination uses slit lamp biomicroscopy and indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression, adding B-scan ultrasonography when visualization is inadequate. If no break is identified, follow-up timing requires judgment: peripheral breaks or detachments may emerge later, or existing pathology may have been missed. Earlier studies reported delayed retinal pathology in 1% to 3% of eyes following an initial PVD; the authors regard their finding of 2.42% with a delayed break or detachment after symptomatic PVD as consistent with those reports. The American Academy of Ophthalmology Preferred Practice Pattern Guidelines published in 2019 advocated another examination within 2 months of presentation, or within 1 to 2 weeks for eyes with vitreous hemorrhage or after treatment of an acute retinal tear. In a study of 7522 patients with acute symptomatic PVD, Seider et al reported a median of 22 days to delayed break or detachment, suggesting that reassessment might be needed earlier than the general 2-month interval. That study identified male sex, age < 60 years, vitreous hemorrhage, lattice degeneration, a fellow-eye history of tear or detachment, and previous cataract surgery as risk factors. Uhr et al studied 7999 eyes with acute symptomatic PVD: 2.6% had a delayed retinal break, at a median of 35 days, and vitreous hemorrhage and male gender were significant risk factors. The authors state that their dataset was the largest known to them for studying the incidence and timing of delayed PVD-associated retinal pathology. Their findings emphasize that ocular risk factors may increase incidence and shorten the interval before pathology develops. With at least 1 of vitreous hemorrhage, lattice degeneration, fellow-eye break/detachment history, or myopia, median times to break and detachment were 34 and 39 days; with vitreous hemorrhage alone, median time to break was 14 days. Previous evidence places the retinal-tear rate with vitreous hemorrhage during acute symptomatic PVD at 70% to 80%. In this setting, bleeding may result from tractional avulsion of superficial retinal vessels or rupture of vessels spanning a tear. A subsequently detected break or detachment could reflect ongoing PVD or incomplete visualization of the vitreous base. B-scan ultrasonography alongside a detailed clinical examination may help identify a break, although reported sensitivity and positive predictive value vary widely (24%e 100%) with the equipment and examiner. For these patients, the authors advise frequent repeat examinations and consideration of early vitrectomy to guard against worsening disease. Myopia has often been identified as a retinal-detachment risk factor, with more severe myopia linked to higher rates of retinal pathology; the authors describe peripheral retinal thinning and premature vitreous liquefaction leading to PVD as contributing factors. In a study by Vitale et al, United States prevalence of moderate myopia ( 2.0 to 7.9 D) rose from 11.4% in 1972 to 22.4% in 2004, while high myopia (more than 8.0 D) increased 8-fold over that period. The authors therefore consider knowledge of precorrected refractive error prudent when assessing retinal-pathology risk after acute PVD. By treating-physician specialty, the interval to delayed break was significantly shorter for nonretinal specialists (median = 37 days) than retinal specialists (median = 42 days) (P < 0.001). The discussion reports no significant difference in time to detachment: median = 49 days for retinal specialists versus median = 56 days for nonretinal specialists (P = 0.39). The article’s Table 2 instead lists 55 days as the nonretinal-specialist median for detachment. The authors suggest that differing symptom counseling, return precautions, and customary follow-up patterns could contribute to timing differences. Limitations include possible IRIS Registry inaccuracies from ICD or procedure-coding errors that could incorrectly include or exclude patients. Acute PVD was identified through ICD codes without individual confirmation by chart review, OCT, or ultrasound. Requiring an extended ophthalmoscopy code could select eyes in which clinicians were more suspicious of pathology and could lead to inappropriate exclusions. Nevertheless, the authors judged their approach more specific than relying on PVD coding alone or on an arbitrary period of prior examinations without a PVD code. With the latter approach, different providers might have failed to code an existing PVD or might not have dilated the eye sufficiently. The database lacked measures of the number of retinal tears, vitreous-hemorrhage severity, and degree of lattice degeneration or myopia. Stratification by severity might have clarified incidence and timing and assisted clinical decisions. Disease found after the initial PVD might also have been present but unrecognized at the first examination; the authors note that this issue is not exclusive to large retrospective database studies. Their methods could not evaluate photopsias, myodesopsias, or examination findings without codes, such as vitreous pigment. Despite these limitations, the authors describe their cohort as the largest known to date for evaluating the timing and frequency of delayed PVD-associated retinal pathology. They consider their findings broadly consistent with the 2019 Academy Preferred Practice Pattern Guidelines and note that the heterogeneous dataset includes records from retinal specialists, comprehensive ophthalmologists, and optometrists. They conclude that PVD is common and usually self-limited but can have severe consequences if managed improperly. Repeat examination is important for detecting delayed retinal disease. They recommend at least one repeat examination within the first 6 weeks for all patients, with earlier and more frequent examinations for eyes with higher-risk features.

document_sections.heading: Unilateral Double Optic Nerve Head Pits with Serous Macular Detachment
document_sections.content: A 29-year-old man had vision of 20/200 in his left eye, which showed 2 separate oval optic disc pits: 1 inferonasal and 1 inferotemporal, with serous macular detachment. Confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscopy and en face OCT angiography images delineated the pits. An OCT B-scan showed intraretinal schisis and serous macular detachment communicating with the inferotemporal pit.
